title: The Tenement Room Where Montessori Counted Forty-Four Repetitions
dek: In January 1907 a Rome housing company asked a physician to keep tenement children off its stairs; she opened a room and watched what they did.

story.company: Casa dei Bambini (Istituto Romano dei Beni Stabili)
story.event: Accepting a housing company's invitation and opening the first Children's House in San Lorenzo
story.summary: Late in 1906 Edoardo Talamo of the Istituto Romano dei Beni Stabili asked the physician Maria Montessori to organise rooms for young children in the company's renovated tenements in San Lorenzo, Rome, where children left alone while their parents worked were damaging the buildings. She accepted, and the first Casa dei Bambini opened on 6 January 1907; her observations there, including a three-year-old repeating an exercise forty-four times, shaped the method she published in 1909. She withdrew from San Lorenzo in 1910 after a conflict with Talamo.
paragraphs: Near the end of 1906, Maria Montessori came back to Rome from Milan, where she had been judging prizes in scientific pedagogy at the International Exhibition. She was a physician who lectured in anthropology at the University of Rome, and for years she had used methods drawn from the French doctors Itard and Seguin to teach children with intellectual disabilities. She had long wanted to try them with ordinary children, she later wrote, but had never thought of starting with the very young.

Then Edoardo Talamo, who ran the Istituto Romano dei Beni Stabili, a company renovating working-class tenements, asked her to organise rooms for small children in its buildings in San Lorenzo, a quarter whose misery filled Rome's newspapers. The reason was practical. Children under school age were left alone all day while their parents worked, and they were damaging the repaired walls and stairs; the money saved on repairs would pay for the room. Montessori later recalled setting conditions on hygiene, food and sanitation before agreeing. There were about fifty children, she said, and no toys and no teacher.

She accepted. The first Casa dei Bambini, the Children's House, opened on 6 January 1907 on Via dei Marsi, in the care of Candida Nuccitelli and under Montessori's direction. She brought materials from her earlier work and watched. During those first trials, she wrote, a girl of about three was fitting wooden cylinders into their holes with such concentration that Montessori began to count. She lifted the chair, girl and all, on to a table and had the other children sing. The girl carried on. After forty-four repetitions she stopped of her own accord and looked round, satisfied. Montessori wrote that "my never-to-be-forgotten impression was that experienced by one who has made a discovery."

A second house opened in San Lorenzo that April, and another in Milan in 1908. In 1909 she wrote the book that became The Montessori Method, published in English in 1912. The partnership did not last: after a conflict with Talamo she withdrew from San Lorenzo in 1910. On the anniversary in 1942 she told her students that what happened there could not have come from her method, "for at the time my method did not yet exist."

quote.text: The prescription is that the subject must be made to show new aspects of itself; to prompt new questions; in a word, to change. From an unchanging subject the attention inevitably wanders away.
quote.work: Talks to Teachers on Psychology; and to Students on Some of Life's Ideals (1899)
quote.source_title: Talks To Teachers On Psychology; And To Students On Some Of Life's Ideals, Project Gutenberg eBook #16287
quote.connection: James, lecturing American teachers in the 1890s, set down the accepted view: attention needs change, or it drifts. Montessori had believed much the same until a three-year-old repeated one unchanging task forty-four times and came out calmer. Perhaps they describe different kinds of attention; the story does not settle it.

reflection: Talamo wanted his stairs left alone. Montessori took that small, practical brief and treated it as a place to watch closely, and the most important thing she saw was nowhere in her plan.

You probably know both kinds of attention James describes: the kind you drag back to a task every few minutes, and the rarer kind that holds by itself. Montessori noticed that the girl came out of her forty-four repetitions looking rested, almost as if from a nap. Not every hour of your day can feel like that. But it is worth knowing which tasks give you that steadiness, and keeping a little time for one of them.
invitation: Choose one task today that you can do without interruption for twenty minutes. Put your phone in another room, do only that, and notice afterwards whether you feel more tired or less.

research_notes: Address: The Montessori Method (1912 translation) prints '58 Via dei Masi', evidently a misprint for Via dei Marsi; Vatican News gives Via dei Marsi 58; Montessori Australia gives 53 Via dei Marsi. The story names only the street. Teacher: the Method names Candida Nuccitelli; Montessori's 1942 address (AMI) speaks of 'a woman of forty years'; the story uses the Method's name. Children's ages: the Method says three to seven, Montessori Australia two to six; the story says only 'under school age'. Number of children: 'some 50' in the 1942 address; the Method does not give a figure for the first room. The forty-four repetitions come only from Montessori's own account in Spontaneous Activity in Education (1917), which places it during her 'first essays' with the children of San Lorenzo without naming the house; the story attributes it to her and does not say it was the first house. Her conditions on hygiene, food and sanitation, the absence of toys and teacher, and her description of herself as a medical officer of hygiene come from her 1942 recollection, attributed as such. Talamo's 1906 invitation: the Method says 'near the end of the year 1906'; Treccani gives 1906. Montessori Australia says she was 'nearly forty' in 1907; she was born on 31 August 1870 (AMS), so 36; the story gives no age. The 'my method did not yet exist' quotation is taken from Montessori Australia's quotation of her 1942 anniversary talk. Smithsonian Magazine (Sonja Anderson) was found but blocks automated requests. The William James passage is from his lectures to teachers on classroom attention, published in 1899; it is set against Montessori's observation, not applied to her directly.
